Avoid wording that suggests a partnership or endorsement, such as "Official OpenSeal partner" or "Certified by OpenSeal", unless the project has agreed to it in writing. Using OpenSeal does not mean your product is endorsed, certified, sponsored or maintained by the OpenSeal project or CasualOffice, and the OpenSeal name and logo are not to be used as your product's own.

These are the conditions of the Apache License 2.0 (section 4), not project policy. When you redistribute OpenSeal or a work derived from it, in source or binary form: give recipients a copy of the LICENSE ; keep the copyright, patent, trademark and attribution notices from the source you received; mark files you modified as changed; include the NOTICE file's attribution notices in a reasonable place: a NOTICE file shipped with your product, its documentation, or a third-party notices screen. Running OpenSeal as a hosted service without distributing it does not trigger these conditions. Forks

If OpenSeal helps you, please say so: in an application footer, an About dialog, a settings or acknowledgements page, your documentation, your third-party notices, or an integration listing. This is a request, not a condition; leaving it out does not affect your rights. OpenSeal never adds attribution to your application or to the PDFs it produces.

A logo used as attribution needs a text alternative: alt="Powered by OpenSeal" on the image, or visible text beside a decorative image with alt="" . A link must be reachable by keyboard and have a visible focus style; its accessible name should say where it goes. Text should meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast (4.5:1 for small text). Use the dark-background logo on dark themes. Attribution should never cover content, block interaction, flash, or appear as a pop-up, banner or watermark.

Administrators manage who can use the account, which programs can call the API, and the account's defaults. Everything here is under Admin , and every action is also an API call.

A member signs in to send and manage envelopes; signers never need an account. Each member has a permission profile . Three are built in: Profile Can admin Everything, including users, API clients and account settings sender Create, send and manage envelopes and templates viewer Look at envelopes without changing them Invite user emails a one-time link to set a password. Resend invitation sends a new link; earlier links stop working. Or add a user with a password (at least 12 characters), or none for someone who signs in another way. Disable sign-in stops a member signing in or calling the API

API clients: personal keys and OAuth clients with their scopes. A program calls the API with one of two kinds of credential: API key ( osk_… ), sent as a bearer token. Good for scripts. OAuth client : a client id and secret exchanged at /api/v1/oauth/token (client-credentials grant) for a one-hour access token signed by the server. Good for services; the keys that verify tokens are at /.well-known/jwks.json . Each client gets only the scopes it needs and an expiry between 1 and 3,650 days. The secret is shown once, when it is created, and stored only as a hash; copy it then. Revoke stops it at

Another site may show OpenSeal's signing, prepare and correct views in a frame, or through the <openseal-signing> and <openseal-prepare> elements, only if its origin is on the workspace's list. Organization, Embedding edits the list, which is a security setting: a staff session needs a recent sign-in to change it. The API's PATCH /accounts/me sets the same list as settings.embedding_origins . At most 20 origins, each written as a browser compares it: https://host or https://host:port , lower case, with no path. Every change to settings, members, groups, profiles, workspaces and the organization is recorded in a hash-chained log in the same transaction as the change. Audit log lists it and exports it as JSON or CSV. Nothing in it is ever edited or deleted.

Each account is a workspace inside an organization. A person in several workspaces switches between them from the sidebar's workspace menu. Organization owners and administrators see the organization's workspaces, people, administrators and its own audit log.

Settings : the account name, after how many days new envelopes expire, and when the first reminder goes out. Branding : the name recipients see in emails and on the signing page, and an accent colour. Text on that colour must stay readable; the form says so if it would not. The OpenSeal API is a JSON REST API over HTTPS. Everything the web app does, it does through this API: 182 public operations, from creating and sending an envelope to reading its sealed documents and audit trail. Pre-release. OpenSeal is a deterministic, headless agreement engine in Rust, hosted by a server of record. The engine owns the PDF, the fields, the routing rules, the seal and the evidence. The server owns identity, storage, delivery, keys and policy. Every arrow leaving the deployment goes through a host seam; the engine knows none of them exist.

OpenSeal's sister projects, OpenCalc and OpenPresent, are document editors where the file is the product and a server only orders edits. In an e-signature product the product is the evidence that the file was agreed to , no party may hold the only copy of it, and no party trusts another. So the engine-and-host split is kept, and the server becomes the system of record.

Upload, admit (bounded parse, active content removed, a report), store the original and its hash, prepare recipients and fields, validate, send. The document hash is fixed and the first recipients are invited.
The link, authentication, consent, the exact bytes whose hash is in the chain, fields validated by the engine in the browser and again on the server, adopt, review, finish. The workflow advances.

The last action moves the envelope to completing . The worker flattens values, adds the certificate and the audit trail, has keyd sign the digest, timestamps it, optionally adds long-term validation data, verifies the result, stores it and records envelope.completed with the sealed hash.
Anyone with the PDF runs the same verifier in the browser or on the command line, against the roots they trust. No server is involved.

h: Are signatures made with OpenSeal legally binding?
t: OpenSeal is designed to support electronic-signature laws such as ESIGN and UETA in the United States and eIDAS in the European Union. Whether a particular signature is valid depends on the deployment, its configuration, the jurisdiction and the transaction. Nothing on this site is legal advice; ask counsel for your case.

h: Is it certified for SOC 2, ISO 27001 or 21 CFR Part 11?
t: No. A self-hosted deployment is certified by its operator, not by the software. OpenSeal plans control mappings to help operators ( LEG-04 ) and a Part 11 mode ( VS-19 ); neither is a certification.

h: Does it support qualified electronic signatures (QES)?
t: Not yet. Remote signing through a qualified trust service provider with the CSC API is planned ( VS-18 ).

h: Can I use OpenSeal in a commercial or closed-source product?
t: Yes. It is licensed under Apache-2.0: you may use, modify, embed, host and sell products built with it, with no royalties and no separate commercial licence. When you redistribute it, keep the LICENSE and the NOTICE file. See brand and attribution .

h: Do I have to show "Powered by OpenSeal"?
t: No. It is appreciated, never required, and OpenSeal never adds it to your application or your PDFs.

h: Why not use an existing open-source project?
t: The established open-source e-signature projects (DocuSeal, Documenso, OpenSign by OpenSign Labs, LibreSign) are licensed under the AGPL, which many companies cannot ship inside their products, and several keep features such as conditional fields, bulk send or SSO in paid editions. OpenSeal is permissively licensed and plans every feature for the open core. OpenSeal is written clean-room: no code from those projects is copied or adapted.

h: How can someone check a document without OpenSeal?
t: The sealed PDF is standard PAdES, so independent validators such as pyHanko and EU DSS check it, and OpenSeal's own verifier runs offline in a browser or on the command line. See Verifying a document .

h: What happens if the OpenSeal server disappears?
t: Every party already holds the sealed PDF with its certificate of completion and audit trail inside, protected by the seal and a trusted timestamp. Nothing needs the server to be verified.

h: Where are the signing keys kept?
t: In keyd, a separate service that uses your HSM through PKCS#11 and signs digests only. See Signing keys .

Yes: a REST API under /api/v1 , described in OpenAPI, with API keys, OAuth 2.1 (authorization code with PKCE, client credentials), the JWT grant, sandbox workspaces, idempotency keys, ETags for safe concurrent edits, and signed webhooks with a delivery log. TypeScript and Python clients are generated from the same contract (in the repository, not yet published). See the API reference and Webhooks .

h: Is the API compatible with DocuSign's?
t: Its concepts are the familiar ones (envelopes, recipients, routing orders, fields, templates, embedded views). A DocuSign-shaped compatibility endpoint is a separate, later question, to be decided with counsel ( VS-25 ).

h: Can I embed signing in my application?
t: Embedded signing, prepare and correct views, the <openseal-signing> and <openseal-prepare> elements and per-workspace allowed origins are built and in review ( VS-09 ); an administrator lists the sites allowed to frame them under Embedding origins .
An envelope is one or more documents, the people who act on them, and the fields each of them fills. You prepare it in four steps: documents, recipients, fields, then review and send.

From Home , drop a PDF or a Word ( .docx ) document on the page or choose Start and then Send for signature . Each recipient has a name, an email address, a type and a routing order. Signers fill fields and sign. Carbon copies receive the completed documents and take no action. Routing order decides who goes when: recipients with order 1 are invited first, order 2 when every order-1 recipient has finished, and so on. Give two signers the same order to let them sign in parallel. The product is not the PDF; it is the proof that the PDF was agreed to. A completed agreement must show which document every party saw, who signed it, when and how, and anyone must be able to check that offline for decades. This page explains how, and what is still to be reviewed. OpenSeal is designed to support electronic-signature laws such as ESIGN, UETA and eIDAS. It makes no claim of legal validity, compliance or certification. An external security and cryptographic review ( SEC-REV-01 ) is a release gate still ahead, and the ASVS self-assessment ( SEC-ASVS-01 ) is written with its findin

Nobody in an agreement trusts anybody else, so the design assumes each of them may attack the record: a signer who later says "I never signed", or tries to change the document after signing; a sender who wants a signer to agree to something other than what they saw; a counterparty holding the PDF who alters it while keeping a valid look (shadow and incremental-saving attacks); another tenant on the same install, an outside attacker , a malicious integrator abusing webhooks or embedded views; an insider or compromised operator who would rewrite evidence, backdate, or sign with the platform key.

Like DocuSign and SignNow by default, OpenSeal separates the person's electronic signature (a typed, drawn or uploaded mark adopted with intent, plus the evidence of who adopted it) from the platform's digital signature , the seal: a cryptographic signature over the final bytes that proves the record has not changed since. Signatures made with each signer's own certificate, for advanced and qualified signatures, are planned ( VS-18 ).

PAdES baseline profiles. B-T is the default: a CAdES-detached CMS signature with an RFC 3161 timestamp from a timestamp authority, so the time does not come from our clock. B-LT adds the certificates and revocation data needed to validate years later without a network; B-LTA adds a document timestamp over everything, renewed before algorithms or certificates weaken. The seal key lives in keyd , a separate daemon that talks PKCS#11 to an HSM (SoftHSM in development). It receives the encoded signed attributes, never the document, and returns the signature. h: Compose says a variable is required
t: Symptom: required variable OPENSEAL_PUBLIC_URL is missing a value: set OPENSEAL_PUBLIC_URL (https) . Fix: the production profile refuses to render until every required variable is set. The configuration reference lists them; set them in your environment or an --env-file .

h: keyd or the worker refuses to start: CS-KEY-0014
t: Log: start_failed with "code":"CS-KEY-0014" naming a setting, and a security_configuration line whose manifest is not matches . Cause: a security setting differs from the recorded manifest, is set but not listed, or is listed but not set. init-secrets.sh leaves both manifests empty, so this is expected until you record them. After a change you did not intend, find what changed first. Fix: after an approved change, record the manifests again and restart: docker compose $F run --rm --no-deps keyd config-manifest | sudo tee "$OPENSEAL_SECRETS_DIR/keyd-config-manifest" > /dev/null docker compose $

Log: the worker logs keyd_unavailable at start, and later transport.backend_failed with CS-KEY-0011 ; envelopes wait in completing ; a seal_failed alert repeats. Cause: keyd is stopped, still starting, or not on the worker's network (connection refused, reset or timed out, or the name does not resolve). This is treated as an outage: the worker keeps running every other job and retries the seal every 60 seconds. Fix: bring keyd back ( docker compose ps keyd , then its log). The next seal attempt completes the envelope; nothing needs to be re-sent.

h: keyd refuses the worker: CS-KEY-0013, CS-KEY-0001
t: Log: the worker stops at start with start_failed and CS-KEY-0013 (the TLS handshake was refused), or CS-KEY-0001 (keyd answered, but the caller is not on its allow list); keyd logs transport.caller_refused with reason handshake or not_allowed and the certificate's fingerprint. Cause: a configuration error, not an outage: OPENSEAL_KEYD_CA is not the CA keyd's certificate chains to, OPENSEAL_KEYD_SERVER_NAME is not the name in keyd's certificate, or the worker's client certificate is untrusted, expired or missing from keyd-allow-list . Fix: compare the fingerprint keyd logged with keyd-allow-lis

h: keyd cannot use the HSM: CS-KEY-0003, CS-KEY-0006
t: Log: keyd's start_failed with CS-KEY-0003 (the HSM is unavailable, the PIN was refused, or a PKCS#11 call failed) or CS-KEY-0006 (no usable certificate, the key not found or ambiguous in the token, or the key does not match the certificate). Fix: check that OPENSEAL_PKCS11_MODULE is inside OPENSEAL_PKCS11_DIR and loads in a slim Linux container, that the token label and key label are exact, that keyd-pkcs11-pin holds the PIN with no trailing newline your HSM rejects, that a network HSM is reachable from keyd's network, and that seal-chain.pem starts with the certificate of that key.

Log: keyd records CS-KEY-0015 ; the worker logs transport.backend_failed with that code and retries every 60 seconds. Cause: keyd holds a seal token key and the database has none, a different one, or a clock more than five minutes from keyd's. Fix: write the same key to keyd-seal-token-key and migrate-seal-token-key , run docker compose $F run --rm migrate (it installs the key), restart keyd, and keep both hosts' clocks on NTP.

h: The timestamp authority fails: CS-WRK-0018, CS-SEAL-0005
t: Log: transport.backend_failed with "backend":"tsa" , the TSA's index in your list and a reason : connect , tls , timeout , status , answer or address_refused (the URL is never logged). The worker tries the next TSA in the list; when none answers, the seal fails and is retried. connect , timeout : the worker cannot reach it. On the production profile only the worker has a route out, through the egress network; check your firewall. tls : the TSA's HTTPS certificate does not verify. answer or CS-SEAL-0005 : the token is not usable. A completed agreement carries its own proof. Anyone holding the sealed PDF can check it, with no account and without asking the server that made it.

The seal : the byte ranges it covers, the digest, the CMS signature, and the certificate chain up to a root you trust. The timestamp : when the seal was made, from an RFC 3161 timestamp authority rather than the server's clock. Every later revision : anything appended after the seal must be of a kind the seal allows (for example long-term validation data). Anything else, including the hiding and replacing tricks known as shadow attacks, makes the document fail. The audit trail embedded as audit-trail.json : every event's hash, its link to the one before, and the sequence.

Outcome Means Signed and unchanged Every signature checks out, and nothing changed after signing except what the signatures allow. Indeterminate Nothing failed, but something could not be confirmed: usually the issuer is not among your trusted certificates. Failed A signature does not verify, or the document was changed in a way its signatures do not allow. Treat it as altered.

OpenSeal tells your system when something happens to an envelope by POSTing a small, signed JSON event to an HTTPS endpoint you register. Events carry ids and statuses only; your system fetches the details it needs with its own credentials.

A subscription names the URL, the event types (or * for all), and references to one to four secrets. Secrets are provisioned by the operator, as an environment variable or a file the worker can read, so they never travel through the API. A secret is whsec_ followed by base64 of at least 16 random bytes. Optionally, limit the subscription to one envelope. curl https://sign.example.com/api/v1/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENSEAL_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: crm-webhook-1" \ -d '{ "url": "https://crm.example.com/hooks/openseal", "event_types": ["enve

Events mirror the audit trail's types that matter to integrators: Envelope: envelope.sent , envelope.delivered , envelope.completing (sealing has started), envelope.completed , envelope.declined , envelope.voided , envelope.expired , envelope.corrected , envelope.purged Recipient: recipient.sent , recipient.delivered , recipient.auth_failed , recipient.completed , recipient.declined , recipient.reassigned , recipient.bounced Designed but not emitted yet: recipient.finish_later , template.* and bulk_send.completed .

{ "id": "0193a1b2-…", "type": "envelope.completed", "created_at": "2026-11-12T09:14:03Z", "account_id": "0193a1b2-…", "data": { "envelope_id": "0193a1b2-…", "status": "completed", "version": 7, "recipient_id": "0193a1b2-…" } } No names, email addresses, subjects, field values or documents are sent, so a misconfigured endpoint leaks nothing about the agreement. recipient_id appears on recipient events. Every attempt of one event sends the same bytes.

Deliveries follow the Standard Webhooks scheme. Three headers come with each request: webhook-id : the event delivery's id, the same on every retry; use it to ignore duplicates. webhook-timestamp : the attempt's Unix time; reject anything more than five minutes old. webhook-signature : v1, and the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of id.timestamp.body , once per active secret, separated by spaces (so secrets can be rotated). import base64, hashlib, hmac, time def verify(secret: str, headers: dict, body: bytes) -> bool: key = base64.b64decode(secret.removeprefix("whsec_")) msg_id, ts = headers["webhook-id"],

Any 2xx answer within 10 seconds counts as delivered. Redirects are not followed. Otherwise the worker retries with exponential back-off (from 30 seconds, doubling, capped at 12 hours, with jitter) for 15 attempts, about three days. Delivery is at least once: the same event may arrive twice with the same webhook-id . Order is not guaranteed; compare version to discard stale events.

Only https:// URLs to public addresses. Private, loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata), carrier-grade NAT, reserved and multicast addresses are refused, both when the address is resolved and again when the connection is made, so DNS rebinding cannot reach your internal network. An operator can allow a private range with OPENSEAL_WEBHOOK_ALLOW . Built: editing, pausing and resuming a subscription, a test delivery, and manual redelivery, from the API and from Admin. h: A seal inside the PDF itself
t: PAdES is the European standard for digital signatures in PDF files. The seal travels with the document, and any PDF validator that knows the standard can read it, not only ours. So: the proof does not depend on OpenSeal still existing. RFC 3161

h: A time nobody can quietly change
t: A timestamp authority, an independent service, signs the moment the seal was made. The time does not come from our clock or yours, so it cannot be backdated later without the timestamp failing. So: "when" is proven, not claimed. Offline verification

Every check uses only the file: whether a byte changed, who sealed it, when, and what was added afterwards. It runs in a browser or on the command line, with no account and no network. So: the other party, an auditor or a court can check it themselves. These are technical properties. Whether a signature is legally effective depends on the jurisdiction, the transaction and how a deployment is run; OpenSeal is designed to support e-signature laws such as ESIGN, UETA and eIDAS and makes no claim of legal validity, compliance or certification.

If you find a weakness in OpenSeal, please tell us privately first, so it can be fixed before it is used against anyone.
Do not open a public issue for a suspected vulnerability, a malicious PDF, a signature-forgery technique, or a real signed agreement.

Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting for the OpenSeal repository. Include: the affected revision (a commit id); the subsystem: PDF reader, sealing, verification, the signing ceremony, the API, keyd, the platform console, or the model service; the impact and a realistic attack path; a minimal reproduction without personal data or real agreements . We will acknowledge the report, assess it, coordinate a fix and an advisory, and credit you if you wish.
